newsitem.title: USA: TALKING POINT - Invesco deal to be watched.
newsitem.headline: TALKING POINT - Invesco deal to be watched.

text.p: Overseas firms will move cautiously in buying U.S. mutual fund companies after Invesco Plc's record-setting purchase of AIM Management Group.
While they will be tempted by the chance to lasso more assets, the expected reticence involves price.

"I don't think it's terribly likely," said Peter Di Terasa, equity fund analyst at Morningstar Inc about more deals in the near future. "What we would probably see is firms waiting to see how this works out."
"People are going to be reluctant to leap in," said Di Terasa. "If this is a pattern setter, it means that foreign investors are going to have to pay up."
And that's not a given, he added.

Overseas firms are reluctant to start their own U.S. fund subsidiaries, in part because of the mammoth marketing and distribution expenses. With the purchase, Invesco saves the time and expense of building an American fund business.
But other potential buyers will study the merger to see how quickly Invesco can digest the deal before they test the waters.
"Whether we have more deals will be a function of whether people will step up and pay these prices," said Michael Lipper, president of Lipper Analytical Services.
Unless there is a way to bring cost efficiencies in quickly, future buyers will only window shop.
Analysts and investment bankers have speculated that European banks, especially German ones, would be eager to buy in part to gather more managed assets.
"Banks are looking for a way to increase fee income," Brewington said. "It's a way to get stable earnings going forward. Asset management gives stable cash flow."
"It's a difficult concept for them to understand spending a great deal of money on marketing," Lipper said. "They don't do that in their home country."
Analysts noted the Invesco-AIM deal was an especially good fit because Invesco was geared toward the institutional side of the business, while AIM had a strong retail fund business.
"They're buying themselves into the U.S. money management market," said Bruce Brewington, an equity analyst at Putnam, Lovell & Thornton, an investment banking firm in San Francisco.

Fund trackers called the Invesco-AIM deal the largest in U.S. fund history. British fund manager Invesco said on Monday it will pay about $1.6 billion for AIM. The two companies would have about $150 billion under management.
Invesco said it would fund the deal with the issuance of 290 million new shares to AIM shareholders. Invesco would spend another $500 million in cash and debt to fund the deal.

The deal tops Mellon Bank Corp's purchase of Dreyfus Funds in 1993. While the deal was valued at $1.8 billion, analysts knocked the total price down to about $1.2 billion, due to about $658 million in cash on Dreyfus' balance sheet.
